fixes.explanation: That's the one, baker. The passage says, “…the kings of the Medes, their governors and all their officials, and all the lands they rule.” Those kings get prepared for battle alongside the kingdoms named just before. Notice the list reaches past the kings to their officials and the lands they rule.

Assyria is a big name, friend, and I bet it jumped right out at you. But it isn't named in these verses. The passage says “…the kings of the Medes…” get prepared, along with their governors, officials and all the lands they rule. Assyria sat this list out.

True, baker. The passage says, “The earth quakes and writhes because the LORD’s intentions against Babylon stand…” Even the earth feels it when the LORD's intentions stand. I think I'd be shaking right alongside it, and I'm standing on a gold base.

A city of refuge would be a nice ending, friend, but that's not what the verse says. The LORD's intentions are to make Babylon's land “…a desolation, without inhabitant.” Earlier in the passage, the nations are summoned against her. This one is not a welcome mat.
That's it, baker. The verse says, “…the bars of her gates are broken.” The warriors are sitting in their strongholds at the same time. Gate bars are what hold a gate shut, and these ones are broken.

The verse doesn't mention temples, friend. It says, “…the bars of her gates are broken.” Bars belong on gates, because they're what keeps a gate shut. In this verse, it's the gates' bars that are broken.

I bet that's the news the king would love to get, friend. But the verse says the opposite. The messengers announce “…that his city has been captured from end to end.” Nothing in this passage says his army wins.

Nice dream, baker, but the verse says something else. The nations were summoned against Babylon, and the messengers carry news that the king's city “…has been captured from end to end.” That's not news of anyone going home. I think those couriers are not carrying good news.

This one is false, friend. The verse says, “The fords have been seized, the marshes set on fire, and the soldiers are terrified.” Terrified is the opposite of calm. Seized fords, burning marshes and terrified soldiers all show up in that one verse.

Correct, baker. The text says the soldiers are terrified. The verse reads, “The fords have been seized, the marshes set on fire, and the soldiers are terrified.” Terrified is about as far from calm as you can get.

Right, baker. The speaker says, “Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon has devoured me; he has crushed me.” The next verse has words from the dweller of Zion and from Jerusalem. I think this is a heavy line, and it's okay to let it be heavy.

That's the opposite of what she says, friend. The speaker says Nebuchadnezzar “…has devoured me; he has crushed me.” The next line says he set her aside “…like an empty vessel…” This is a complaint, and a painful one.

That's right, baker. The dweller of Zion says, “May the violence done to me and to my flesh be upon Babylon…” Then Jerusalem says, “May my blood be on the dwellers of Chaldea…” I think these are heavy words.

Edom isn't mentioned here, baker. The dweller of Zion says, “May the violence done to me and to my flesh be upon Babylon…” Then Jerusalem says, “May my blood be on the dwellers of Chaldea…” Edom isn't in either one.
Yes, baker. The LORD says, “Behold, I will plead your case and take vengeance on your behalf…” Notice the word "I" in that line. The LORD says it right after Jerusalem's words.

Grain isn't in this verse, friend, though a threshing floor and a harvest came up earlier in the passage (Jeremiah 51:33). Here the LORD says, “Babylon will become a heap of rubble, a haunt for jackals…” Rubble is what's piled up, not grain.

That's right, baker. The LORD says, “then they will fall asleep forever and never wake up, declares the LORD.” The feast comes first, and then the sleep that has no morning. I think this is a heavy line.

True, baker. The verse says, “The praise of all the earth has been seized. What a horror Babylon has become among the nations!” The verse sets the praise of all the earth right beside the horror Babylon has become. That's quite a drop.

That's right, friend. The verse says, “Her cities have become a desolation, a dry and arid land, a land where no one lives, where no son of man passes through.” Dry and arid is a long way from a green land full of fields. It's dry, and no one lives there.
The verse doesn't say anything about distance, baker. It says, “The nations will no longer stream to him…” No longer means the streaming stops. Bel doesn't get a bigger line out the door.
The wall doesn't stay up, friend. The LORD says, “even the wall of Babylon will fall.” The wall is one more thing that goes down. So that statement doesn't match the verse.
